root.note: That casa is Latin is certain. Where Latin got it is not: scholars suspect a loan from an older language. The Hebrew origin proposed by a Spanish dictionary of the 1600s is rejected today.

history: Your casa began as something much smaller. In classical Latin a casa was a hut or cottage: Isidore of Seville, writing around the year 600, describes a shelter of stakes and branches against cold and heat. Only in Late and Medieval Latin did the word come to mean any dwelling, and Spanish kept that meaning. It has grown a useful family. Your casero is your landlord, and casarse, ‘to get married’, is probably built on casa too, as if you were joining a household. Don't confuse it with caja, ‘box’: that comes from a different Latin word, capsa.
historyEinfach: Casa is a Latin word. In Latin it meant a small, simple house: a hut. Later it meant any house, and Spanish kept this meaning. The word casero, ‘landlord’, comes from casa. The verb casarse, ‘to get married’, probably comes from casa too. When you marry, you join a house.

elsewhere.text: Italian kept the same Latin word with the same spelling, so a Spanish and an Italian casa look identical. Portuguese has casa too.
